==== Human cloning ====
{{Main|Human cloning}}
Human cloning is the creation of a genetically identical copy of a human. The term is generally used to refer to artificial human cloning, which is the reproduction of human cells and tissues. It does not refer to the natural conception and delivery of [[monozygotic|identical]] [[multiple birth|twins]]. The possibility of human cloning has raised [[ethics of cloning|controversies]]. These ethical concerns have prompted several nations to pass legislation regarding human cloning and its legality. As of right now, scientists have no intention of trying to clone people and they believe their results should spark a wider discussion about the laws and regulations the world needs to regulate cloning.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Martinez|first1=Bobby|title=Watch: Scientists clone monkeys using technique that created Dolly the sheep|url=http://fox61.com/2018/01/25/watch-scientists-clone-monkeys-using-technique-that-created-dolly-the-sheep/|website=Fox61|publisher=WTIC-TV|access-date=26 January 2018|date=26 January 2018}}</ref>

Two commonly discussed types of theoretical human cloning are ''therapeutic cloning'' and ''reproductive cloning''. Therapeutic cloning would involve cloning cells from a human for use in medicine and transplants, and is an active area of research, but is not in medical practice anywhere in the world, {{as of|2024|lc=y}}. Two common methods of therapeutic cloning that are being researched are [[somatic-cell nuclear transfer]] and, more recently, [[Induced pluripotent stem cell|pluripotent stem cell induction]]. Reproductive cloning would involve making an entire cloned human, instead of just specific cells or tissues.<ref name="ncbi.nlm.nih.gov">{{cite journal | pmid = 18523539 | volume=10 | issue=2 | title=Therapeutic cloning: promises and issues | pmc=2323472 | date=July 2007 | journal=Mcgill J Med | pages=112–20 | last1 = Kfoury | first1 = C}}</ref>

==== Ethical issues of cloning ====
{{Main|Ethics of cloning}}

There are a variety of [[bioethics|ethical]] positions regarding the possibilities of cloning, especially [[human cloning]]. While many of these views are religious in origin, the questions raised by cloning are faced by secular perspectives as well. Perspectives on human cloning are theoretical, as human therapeutic and reproductive cloning are not commercially used; animals are currently cloned in laboratories and in [[livestock]] production.

Advocates support development of therapeutic cloning to generate tissues and whole organs to treat patients who otherwise cannot obtain transplants,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ornl.gov/sci/techresources/Human_Genome/elsi/cloning.shtml#organsQ |title=Cloning Fact Sheet |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130502125744/http://www.ornl.gov/sci/techresources/Human_Genome/elsi/cloning.shtml |publisher=U.S. Department of Energy Genome Program |date=11 May 2009 |archive-date=2 May 2013}}</ref> to avoid the need for [[immunosuppressive drugs]],<ref name="ncbi.nlm.nih.gov"/> and to stave off the effects of aging.<ref name=EndingAging>de Grey, Aubrey; Rae, Michael (September 2007). ''Ending Aging: The Rejuvenation Breakthroughs that Could Reverse Human Aging in Our Lifetime''. New York, NY: St. Martin's Press, 416 pp. {{ISBN|0-312-36706-6}}.</ref> Advocates for reproductive cloning believe that parents who cannot otherwise procreate should have access to the technology.<ref>''Times Higher Education''. 10 August 2001 [https://www.timeshighereducation.co.uk/164313.article In the news: Antinori and Zavos]</ref>

Opponents of cloning have concerns that technology is not yet developed enough to be safe<ref>{{cite web| url = http://www.aaas.org/spp/sfrl/docs/cloningstatement.shtml| title = AAAS Statement on Human Cloning| access-date = 6 June 2007| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120911093343/http://www.aaas.org/spp/sfrl/docs/cloningstatement.shtml| archive-date = 11 September 2012}}</ref> and that it could be prone to abuse (leading to the generation of humans from whom organs and tissues would be harvested),<ref name="McGee">{{cite web |last=McGee |first=G. |title=Primer on Ethics and Human Cloning |date=October 2011 |publisher=American Institute of Biological Sciences |url=http://www.actionbioscience.org/biotech/mcgee.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130223142719/http://www.actionbioscience.org/biotech/mcgee.html |archive-date=23 February 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |publisher=UNESCO |date=11 November 1997 |url=http://portal.unesco.org/en/ev.php-URL_ID=13177&URL_DO=DO_TOPIC&URL_SECTION=201.html |title=Universal Declaration on the Human Genome and Human Rights |access-date=27 February 2008}}</ref> as well as concerns about how cloned individuals could integrate with families and with society at large.<ref>McGee, Glenn (2000). ''The Perfect Baby: Parenthood in the New World of Cloning and Genetics''. Lanham: Rowman & Littlefield.</ref><ref name="Human Cloning Ethics">{{cite journal| author=Havstad JC| title=Human reproductive cloning: a conflict of liberties | journal=Bioethics | year= 2010 | volume= 24 | issue= 2 | pages= 71–7 | pmid=19076121 | doi=10.1111/j.1467-8519.2008.00692.x | s2cid=40051820 | url=https://philarchive.org/rec/HAVHRC }}</ref> Cloning humans could lead to serious violations of [[human rights]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Engineering |first1=Berkeley Master of |title=Op-ed: The dangers of cloning |url=https://funginstitute.berkeley.edu/news/op-ed-the-dangers-of-cloning/ |website=Fung Institute for Engineering Leadership |access-date=8 March 2023 |date=11 May 2020}}</ref>

Religious groups are divided, with some opposing the technology as usurping "God's place" and, to the extent embryos are used, destroying a human life; others support therapeutic cloning's potential life-saving benefits.<ref>Bob Sullivan, Technology correspondent for NBC News. November 262003 [https://web.archive.org/web/20131214225206/http://www.nbcnews.com/id/3076930/#.UqzUNmRDuxg Religions reveal little consensus on cloning – Health – Special Reports – Beyond Dolly: Human Cloning]</ref><ref>Bainbridge, William Sims (October 2003). [https://www.jetpress.org/volume13/bainbridge.html "Religious Opposition to Cloning"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180421110212/https://www.jetpress.org/volume13/bainbridge.html |date=21 April 2018 }}. ''[[Journal of Evolution and Technology]]''. '''13'''.</ref> There is at least one religion, [[Raëlism#Cloning and survival after death|Raëlism]], in which cloning plays a major role<!-- (in this case in a passive as well as in a proactive/motivational way where cloning is considered positive or negative depending on context or purpose)-->.<ref>{{cite news |title=Out of this world |url=https://www.theguardian.com/education/2002/feb/15/medicalscience.research |access-date=8 March 2023 |work=The Guardian |date=15 February 2002}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Raelian leader says cloning first step to immortality - Feb. 12, 2004 |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2002/HEALTH/12/27/human.cloning/index.html |access-date=8 March 2023 |work=CNN |archive-date=23 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230123174917/http://edition.cnn.com/2002/HEALTH/12/27/human.cloning/index.html }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Zitner |first1=Aaron |title=Lawmakers Propose Human Cloning Ban, Alien Order Notwithstanding |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2001-mar-29-mn-44248-story.html |access-date=8 March 2023 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=29 March 2001}}</ref>

Contemporary work on this topic is concerned with the ethics, adequate regulation and issues of any cloning carried out by humans, [[Space law#Spacefaring machines and space colonization|not potentially by extraterrestrials]] (including in the future), and largely also not replication – also described as mind cloning<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Huberman |first1=Jenny |title=Immortality transformed: mind cloning, transhumanism and the quest for digital immortality |journal=Mortality |date=2 January 2018 |volume=23 |issue=1 |pages=50–64 |doi=10.1080/13576275.2017.1304366 |s2cid=152261367 |issn=1357-6275}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mandelbaum |first1=Eric |title=Everything and More: The Prospects of Whole Brain Emulation |journal=Journal of Philosophy |date=2022 |volume=119 |issue=8 |pages=444–459 |doi=10.5840/jphil2022119830|s2cid=252266788 |url=https://philpapers.org/rec/MANEAM-4 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Godfrey |first1=Alex |title=The science of Black Mirror's Ashley Too: will 'whole brain emulation' ever be possible? |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/tv/2019/06/06/science-black-mirrors-ashley-will-whole-brain-emulation-ever/ |access-date=8 March 2023 |work=The Telegraph |date=6 June 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Hanson |first1=Robin |title=The age of em: work, love, and life when robots rule the Earth |date=2016 |location=Oxford |isbn=978-0-19-875462-6 |edition=First}}</ref> – of potential whole brain emulations.

Cloning of animals is opposed by animal-groups due to the number of cloned animals that suffer from malformations before they die, and while food from cloned animals has been approved as safe by the US FDA,<ref name=Watanabe>{{cite journal | pmid = 23829575 | doi=10.1111/asj.12087 | volume=84 |issue = 9| title=Effect of calf death loss on cloned cattle herd derived from somatic cell nuclear transfer: clones with congenital defects would be removed by the death loss | date=September 2013 | journal=Animal Science Journal | pages=631–8 | last1 = Watanabe | first1 = S}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.nbcnews.com/id/16372490 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130613044122/http://www.nbcnews.com/id/16372490 |archive-date=13 June 2013 |title=FDA says cloned animals are OK to eat |date=28 December 2006 |agency=Associated Press |publisher=[[NBC News]]}}</ref> its use is opposed by groups concerned about food safety.<ref>{{cite web |title=An HSUS Report: Welfare Issues with Genetic Engineering and Cloning of Farm Animals |url=http://www.humanesociety.org/assets/pdfs/farm/hsus-welfare-issues-with-genetic-engineering-and-cloning-of-farm-animals.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101224071552/http://www.humanesociety.org/assets/pdfs/farm/hsus-welfare-issues-with-genetic-engineering-and-cloning-of-farm-animals.pdf |archive-date=2010-12-24 |url-status=live |publisher=[[Humane Society of the United States]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.consumersunion.org/pdf/FDA_clone_comments.pdf |title=Comments of Consumers Union to US Food and Drug Administration on Docket No. 2003N-0573, Draft Animal Cloning Risk Assessment |date=27 April 2007 |first=Michael |last=Hansen |publisher=[[Consumers Union]] |access-date=16 October 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091211051535/http://www.consumersunion.org/pdf/FDA_clone_comments.pdf |archive-date=11 December 2009 }}</ref>

In practical terms, the inclusion of "licensing requirements for embryo research projects and fertility clinics, restrictions on the commodification of eggs and sperm, and measures to prevent proprietary interests from monopolizing access to stem cell lines" in international cloning regulations has been proposed, albeit e.g. effective oversight mechanisms or cloning requirements have not been described.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sandel |first1=Michael J |title=The Ethical Implications of Human Cloning |journal=Perspectives in Biology and Medicine |date=2005 |volume=48 |issue=2 |pages=241–247 |doi=10.1353/pbm.2005.0063 |pmid=15834196 |s2cid=32155922 |issn=1529-8795}}</ref>

==== Cloning extinct and endangered species ====
{{main|De-extinction}}
Cloning, or more precisely, the reconstruction of functional DNA from [[extinct]] species has, for decades, been a dream. Possible implications of this were dramatized in the 1984 novel ''[[Carnosaur (novel)|Carnosaur]]'' and the 1990 novel ''[[Jurassic Park (novel)#Biological issues and accuracy|Jurassic Park]]''.<ref name=Holt/><ref name="Ehrenfeld">{{cite journal|last=Ehrenfeld|first=David|author-link=David Ehrenfeld|year=2006|title=Transgenics and Vertebrate Cloning as Tools for Species Conservation|journal=Conservation Biology|volume=20|issue=3|pages=723–732|pmid=16909565|doi=10.1111/j.1523-1739.2006.00399.x|bibcode=2006ConBi..20..723E |s2cid=12798003}}</ref> The best current cloning techniques have an average success rate of 9.4 percent<ref>{{cite journal | journal = Biol. Reprod. | date=December 2010 | volume=83 |issue=6 | pages=929–37 | title=Inhibition of class IIb histone deacetylase significantly improves cloning efficiency in mice |vauthors=Ono T, Li C, Mizutani E, Terashita Y, Yamagata K, Wakayama T | pmid = 20686182 | doi=10.1095/biolreprod.110.085282| doi-access=free }}</ref> (and as high as 25 percent<ref name="Wakayama" />) when working with familiar species such as mice,{{refn|group=note|One news article in 2014 reported success rates of 70-80 percent for cloning pigs by [[Beijing Genomics Institute|BGI]], a Chinese company<ref>Shukman, David (14 January 2014) [https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-25576718 China cloning on an 'industrial scale'] BBC News Science and Environment, Retrieved 27 February 2016</ref> and in another news article in 2015 a Korean Company, Sooam Biotech, claimed 40 percent success rates with cloning dogs<ref name="Sooam">{{cite news|last1=Baer|first1=Drake|title=This Korean lab has nearly perfected dog cloning, and that's just the start|url=http://www.techinsider.io/how-woosuk-hwangs-sooam-biotech-mastered-cloning-2015-8|access-date=27 February 2016|work=[[Tech Insider]] |date=8 September 2015}}</ref>}} while cloning wild animals is usually less than 1 percent successful.<ref>Ferris Jabr for Scientific American. 11 March 2013.  [https://www.scientificamerican.com/article.cfm?id=cloning-endangered-animals Will cloning ever saved endangered species?]</ref>

===== De-extinction =====
One of the most anticipated targets for cloning was once the [[woolly mammoth]], but attempts to extract DNA from frozen mammoths have been unsuccessful, though a joint Russo-Japanese team is currently working toward this goal.{{when|date=March 2022}} In January 2011, it was reported by Yomiuri Shimbun that a team of scientists headed by Akira Iritani of Kyoto University had built upon research by Dr. Wakayama, saying that they will extract DNA from a mammoth carcass that had been preserved in a Russian laboratory and insert it into the egg cells of an [[Asian elephant]] in hopes of producing a mammoth embryo. The researchers said they hoped to produce a baby mammoth within six years.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/asia-pacific/3075381.stm|title=Scientists 'to clone mammoth'|work=BBC News|date=18 August 2003}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/technology-16068581 |title=BBC News |publisher=BBC |date=7 December 2011 |access-date=19 August 2012}}</ref> The challenges are formidable. Extensively degraded DNA that may be suitable for sequencing may not be suitable for cloning; it would have to be synthetically reconstituted. In any case, with currently available technology, DNA alone is not suitable for mammalian cloning; intact viable cell nuclei are required. Patching pieces of reconstituted mammoth DNA into an Asian elephant cell nucleus would result in an elephant-mammoth hybrid rather than a true mammoth.<ref name=rure>[http://expert.ru/russian_reporter/2015/05/kogda-oni-vernutsya/ "Когда вернутся мамонты"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150630122510/http://expert.ru/russian_reporter/2015/05/kogda-oni-vernutsya/ |date=30 June 2015 }} ("When the Mammoths Return"), 5 February 2015 (retrieved 6 September 2015)</ref> Moreover, true de-extinction of the wooly mammoth species would require a breeding population, which would require cloning of multiple genetically distinct but reproductively compatible individuals, multiplying both the amount of work and the uncertainties involved in the project. There are potentially other post-cloning problems associated with the survival of a reconstructed mammoth, such as the requirement of [[ruminant]]s for specific [[symbiotic]] [[microbiota]] in their stomachs for digestion.<ref name=rure/>

Scientists at the [[University of Newcastle (Australia)|University of Newcastle]] and [[University of New South Wales]] announced in March 2013 that the very recently extinct [[gastric-brooding frog]] would be the subject of a cloning attempt to resurrect the species.<ref name="National Geographic">{{cite web|last=Yong|first=Ed|title=Resurrecting the Extinct Frog with a Stomach for a Womb|website=[[National Geographic (magazine)|National Geographic]]|date=15 March 2013|url=http://phenomena.nationalgeographic.com/2013/03/15/resurrecting-the-extinct-frog-with-a-stomach-for-a-womb/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130318032939/http://phenomena.nationalgeographic.com/2013/03/15/resurrecting-the-extinct-frog-with-a-stomach-for-a-womb/|archive-date=18 March 2013|access-date=15 March 2013}}</ref>

Many such "de-extinction" projects are being championed by the non-profit [[Revive & Restore]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://longnow.org/revive/ | title=Long Now Foundation, Revive and Restore Project| date=25 May 2017}}</ref>

In 2022, scientists showed major limitations and the scale of challenge of genetic-editing-based de-extinction, suggesting resources spent on more comprehensive de-extinction projects such as [[Woolly mammoth#Revival of the species|of the woolly mammoth]] may currently not be well [[Resource allocation|allocated]] and substantially limited. Their analyses "show that even when the extremely high-quality Norway brown rat ([[R. norvegicus]]) is used as a reference, nearly 5% of the genome sequence is unrecoverable, with 1,661 genes recovered at lower than 90% completeness, and 26 completely absent", complicated further by that "distribution of regions affected is not random, but for example, if 90% completeness is used as the cutoff, genes related to immune response and olfaction are excessively affected" due to which "a reconstructed Christmas Island rat would lack attributes likely critical to surviving in its natural or natural-like environment".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lin |first1=Jianqing |last2=Duchêne |first2=David |last3=Carøe |first3=Christian |last4=Smith |first4=Oliver |last5=Ciucani |first5=Marta Maria |last6=Niemann |first6=Jonas |last7=Richmond |first7=Douglas |last8=Greenwood |first8=Alex D. |last9=MacPhee |first9=Ross |last10=Zhang |first10=Guojie |last11=Gopalakrishnan |first11=Shyam |last12=Gilbert |first12=M. Thomas P. |title=Probing the genomic limits of de-extinction in the Christmas Island rat |journal=Current Biology |date=11 April 2022 |volume=32 |issue=7 |pages=1650–1656.e3 |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2022.02.027 |pmid=35271794 |pmc=9044923 |bibcode=2022CBio...32E1650L |s2cid=247323087 |language=English |issn=0960-9822}}
* News report on the study: {{cite news |last1=Ahmed |first1=Issam |title=Forget mammoths, study shows how to resurrect Christmas Island rats |url=https://phys.org/news/2022-03-mammoths-resurrect-christmas-island-rats.html |access-date=19 April 2022 |work=phys.org |language=en}}</ref>

In a 2021 online session of the Russian Geographical Society, Russia's defense minister [[Sergei Shoigu]] mentioned using the DNA of 3,000-year-old [[Scythians#Warfare|Scythian warriors]] to potentially bring them back to life. The idea was described as absurd at least at this point in news reports and it was noted that Scythians likely weren't skilled warriors by default.<ref>{{cite news |title=Russia Is Going to Try to Clone an Army of 3,000-Year-Old Scythian Warriors |url=https://www.popularmechanics.com/science/archaeology/a36383243/russia-wants-to-clone-ancient-army/ |access-date=8 March 2023 |work=Popular Mechanics |date=11 May 2021 |language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Wehner |first1=Mike |title=Does Russia really think it can clone ancient warriors? |url=https://bgr.com/science/russia-cloning-soldier-scythian/ |access-date=8 March 2023 |work=BGR |date=24 May 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Lang |first1=Fabienne |title=Russia's Defense Minister Wants to Clone 3000-Year-Old Scythian Army |url=https://interestingengineering.com/science/russian-defense-minister-hints-at-cloning-3000-year-old-scythian-army |access-date=8 March 2023 |work=interestingengineering.com |date=14 May 2021}}</ref>

The idea of cloning [[Neanderthals]] or bringing them back to life in general is controversial but some scientists have stated that it may be possible in the future and have outlined several issues or problems with such as well as broad rationales for doing so.<ref>{{cite news |title=Yes, We Should Clone Neanderthals |url=https://www.discovermagazine.com/the-sciences/yes-we-should-clone-neanderthals |access-date=8 March 2023 |work=Discover Magazine |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Could we clone a Neanderthal? |url=https://www.sciencefocus.com/nature/could-we-clone-a-neanderthal/ |access-date=8 March 2023 |work=BBC Science Focus Magazine |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Return of the Neanderthals |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/130306-neanderthal-genome-extinction-cloning-hominid-science |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210217170739/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/130306-neanderthal-genome-extinction-cloning-hominid-science |archive-date=17 February 2021 |access-date=8 March 2023 |work=Science |date=6 March 2013 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Lupkin |first1=Sydney |title=Harvard Prof Says Neanderthal Clones Possible but Experts Doubt It |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Health/harvard-prof-neanderthal-clones-experts-doubt/story?id=18275611 |access-date=8 March 2023 |work=ABC News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Brown |first1=Andrew |title=Should we clone Neanderthals? |url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2011/jun/23/clone-neanderthal-technology-ethical |website=The Guardian |access-date=8 March 2023 |date=23 June 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Lallanilla |first1=Marc |title=Could a Surrogate Mother Deliver a Neanderthal Baby? |url=https://www.livescience.com/26447-neanderthal-clone-church.html |website=livescience.com |access-date=8 March 2023 |language=en |date=21 January 2013}}</ref>

====== Unsuccessful attempts ======
In 2001, a cow named Bessie gave birth to a cloned Asian [[gaur]], an endangered species, but the calf died after two days. In 2003, a [[banteng]] was successfully cloned, followed by three [[African wildcat]]s from a thawed frozen embryo. These successes provided hope that similar techniques (using surrogate mothers of another species) might be used to clone extinct species. Anticipating this possibility, tissue samples from the last ''bucardo'' ([[Pyrenean ibex]]) were frozen in [[liquid nitrogen]] immediately after it died in 2000. Researchers are also considering cloning endangered species such as the [[Giant panda]] and [[Cheetah]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=CNN – Nature – First cloned endangered species dies 2 days after birth – January 12, 2001|url=http://edition.cnn.com/2001/NATURE/01/12/cloned.gaur/|access-date=25 October 2020|work=CNN|archive-date=15 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210415083104/http://edition.cnn.com/2001/NATURE/01/12/cloned.gaur/}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|date=22 November 2013|title=Fresh effort to clone extinct animal|language=en-GB|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-25052233|access-date=25 October 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Endangered Species Cloning|url=https://www.elements.nb.ca/theme/endangeredspecies/cheetah/mediaarticle.htm|access-date=25 October 2020|website=www.elements.nb.ca|archive-date=21 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150921093936/http://www.elements.nb.ca/theme/endangeredspecies/cheetah/mediaarticle.htm}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Khan|first=Firdos Alam|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VIuADwAAQBAJ|title=Biotechnology Fundamentals|date=3 September 2018|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=978-1-315-36239-7|language=en}}</ref>

In 2002, geneticists at the [[Australian Museum]] announced that they had replicated DNA of the [[thylacine]] (Tasmanian tiger), at the time extinct for about 65 years, using [[polymerase chain reaction]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.cnn.com/2002/WORLD/asiapcf/auspac/05/28/aust.thylacines/|title=Cloning to revive extinct species|first=Grant|last=Holloway|work=CNN|date=28 May 2002}}</ref> However, on 15 February 2005 the museum announced that it was stopping the project after tests showed the specimens' DNA had been too badly degraded by the ([[ethanol]]) preservative. On 15 May 2005 it was announced that the thylacine project would be revived, with new participation from researchers in [[New South Wales]] and [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.smh.com.au/national/researchers-revive-plan-to-clone-the-tassie-tiger-20050515-gdlbos.html|title=Researchers revive plan to clone the Tassie tiger|date=15 May 2005|website=The Sydney Morning Herald|language=en|access-date=1 February 2019}}</ref> 
In 2022 [[Colossal Biosciences]] and [[University of Melbourne]] announced further efforts to de-extinct the Thylacine, creating the Thylacine Integrated Genetic Restoration Research (TIGRR) Lab, which claims it has made a series of significant advancements, including having produced a thylacine genome that is "more than 99.9-per-cent accurate".<ref>{{cite news |last1=Whitfield |first1=Meg |title=Tasmanian tiger 'de-extinction' project claims genome breakthrough — but other scientists want to see the data |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-10-17/tasmanian-tiger-thylacine-deextinction-project-genome-sequence/104466948 |access-date=9 January 2026 |work=ABC News |date=17 October 2024 |language=en-AU}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Thylacine Integrated Genomic Restoration Research Lab |url=https://tigrrlab.science.unimelb.edu.au/research/ |publisher=University of Melbourne |access-date=9 January 2026}}</ref>

In 2003, for the first time, an extinct animal, the Pyrenean ibex mentioned above was cloned, at the Centre of Food Technology and Research of Aragon, using the preserved frozen cell nucleus of the skin samples from 2001 and domestic goat egg-cells. The ibex died shortly after birth due to physical defects in its lungs.<ref name="The Telegraph">{{cite news | title =Extinct ibex is resurrected by cloning | url =https://www.telegraph.co.uk/scienceandtechnology/science/sciencenews/4409958/Extinct-ibex-is-resurrected-by-cloning.html | archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20090201152052/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/scienceandtechnology/science/sciencenews/4409958/Extinct-ibex-is-resurrected-by-cloning.html | archive-date =1 February 2009 | access-date = 1 February 2009 |work = The Telegraph | location=London | first1=Richard | last1=Gray | first2=Roger | last2=Dobson | date=31 January 2009}}</ref>

===Lifespan===
After an eight-year project involving the use of a pioneering cloning technique, Japanese researchers created 25 generations of healthy cloned mice with normal lifespans, demonstrating that clones are not intrinsically shorter-lived than naturally born animals.<ref name="Wakayama">{{cite journal| journal=Cell Stem Cell | date = 7 March 2013 | volume=12 |issue=3 | pages=293–7 | title=Successful serial recloning in the mouse over multiple generations |vauthors=Wakayama S, Kohda T, Obokata H, Tokoro M, Li C, Terashita Y, Mizutani E, Nguyen VT, Kishigami S, Ishino F, Wakayama T | pmid = 23472871 | doi=10.1016/j.stem.2013.01.005| doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="gen25">{{cite web |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2013/03/130307122958.htm |title=Generations of Cloned Mice With Normal Lifespans Created: 25th Generation and Counting|website=Science Daily|date=7 March 2013 |access-date=8 March 2013}}</ref> Other sources have noted that the offspring of clones tend to be healthier than the original clones and indistinguishable from animals produced naturally.<ref>{{Cite book |title=The Epigenetics Revolution|last=Carey|first=Nessa|publisher=Icon Books Ltd.|year=2012|isbn=978-184831-347-7|location=London, UK|pages=149–150}}</ref>

Some posited that Dolly the sheep may have aged more quickly than naturally born animals, as she died relatively early for a sheep at the age of six. Ultimately, her death was attributed to a respiratory illness, and the "advanced aging" theory is disputed.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Burgstaller|first1=Jörg Patrick|last2=Brem|first2=Gottfried|date=2017|title=Aging of Cloned Animals: A Mini-Review|journal=Gerontology|language=en|volume=63|issue=5|page=419|doi=10.1159/000452444|pmid=27820924|issn=0304-324X|doi-access=free}}</ref>{{dubious|date=August 2018}}

A 2016 study indicated that once cloned animals survive the first month or two of life they are generally healthy.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sinclair |first1=K. D. |last2=Corr |first2=S. A. |last3=Gutierrez |first3=C. G. |last4=Fisher |first4=P. A. |last5=Lee |first5=J.-H. |last6=Rathbone |first6=A. J. |last7=Choi |first7=I. |last8=Campbell |first8=K. H. S. |last9=Gardner |first9=D. S. |date=2016-07-26 |title=Healthy ageing of cloned sheep |journal=Nature Communications |volume=7 |article-number=12359 |doi=10.1038/ncomms12359 |issn=2041-1723 |pmc=4963533 |pmid=27459299|bibcode=2016NatCo...712359S }}</ref> However, early pregnancy loss and neonatal losses are still greater with cloning than natural conception or assisted reproduction (IVF). Current research is attempting to overcome these problems.<ref name="BBCname" />

==In popular culture==

[[File:Doctor Who Experience London Olympia (5502759139).jpg|thumb|[[Sontaran]]s in ''[[Doctor Who]]'' are a cloned warrior race.]]
Discussion of cloning in the popular media often presents the subject negatively. In an article in the 8 November 1993 article of ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'', cloning was portrayed in a negative way, modifying Michelangelo's ''[[Creation of Adam]]'' to depict Adam with five identical hands.<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |volume=142 |issue=19 |title=Cloning Humans |url=https://content.time.com/time/magazine/0,9263,7601931108,00.html|access-date=5 November 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171105153733/http://content.time.com/time/magazine/0,9263,7601931108,00.html|archive-date=5 November 2017|date=8 November 1993|url-status=live}}</ref> ''[[Newsweek]]''{{'s}} 10 March 1997 issue also critiqued the ethics of human cloning, and included a graphic depicting identical babies in beakers.<ref>{{cite magazine|title=Today The Sheep ...|magazine=[[Newsweek]]|date=9 March 1997|url=https://www.newsweek.com/today-sheep-170570|access-date=5 November 2017|language=en}}</ref>

The concept of cloning, particularly human cloning, has featured a wide variety of science fiction works. An early fictional depiction of cloning is [[Bokanovsky's Process]] which features in [[Aldous Huxley]]'s 1931 dystopian novel ''[[Brave New World]]''. The process is applied to fertilized human [[Egg (biology)|eggs]] ''[[in vitro]]'', causing them to split into identical genetic copies of the original.<ref>Huxley, Aldous; "Brave New World and Brave New World Revisited"; p. 19; HarperPerennial, 2005.</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Bhelkar|first1=Ratnakar D.|title=Science Fiction: Fantasy and Reality|date=2009|publisher=Atlantic Publishers & Dist|isbn=978-81-269-1036-6|page=58|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bvt_NyXYGb0C&pg=PA58|access-date=4 November 2017|language=en}}</ref> Following renewed interest in cloning in the 1950s, the subject was explored further in works such as [[Poul Anderson]]'s 1953 story ''UN-Man'', which describes a technology called "exogenesis", and [[Gordon Rattray Taylor]]'s book ''[[The Biological Time Bomb]]'', which popularised the term "cloning" in 1963.<ref name="stableford">{{cite book|last1=Stableford|first1=Brian M.|title=Science Fact and Science Fiction: An Encyclopedia|date=2006|publisher=Taylor & Francis|isbn=978-0-415-97460-8|pages=[https://archive.org/details/sciencefactscien0000stab/page/91 91–92]|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uefwmdROKTAC&pg=PA91|language=en|chapter=Clone|url=https://archive.org/details/sciencefactscien0000stab/page/91}}</ref>

Cloning is a recurring theme in a number of contemporary science fiction films, ranging from action films such as ''[[Anna to the Infinite Power]]'', ''[[The Boys from Brazil (film)|The Boys from Brazil]]'', ''[[Jurassic Park (film)|Jurassic Park]]'' (1993), ''[[Alien Resurrection]]'' (1997), ''[[The 6th Day]]'' (2000), ''[[Resident Evil (2002 video game)|Resident Evil]]'' (2002), ''[[Star Wars: Episode II – Attack of the Clones]]'' (2002), ''[[The Island (2005 film)|The Island]]'' (2005), ''[[Tales of the Abyss]]'' (2006), and ''[[Moon (2009 film)|Moon]]'' (2009) to comedies such as [[Woody Allen]]'s 1973 film ''[[Sleeper (1973 film)|Sleeper]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0070707/|title=Sleeper (1973)|date=17 December 1973|website=IMDb|access-date=3 May 2015}}</ref>

The process of cloning is represented variously in fiction. Many works depict the artificial creation of humans by a method of growing cells from a tissue or DNA sample; the replication may be instantaneous, or take place through slow growth of human embryos in [[artificial womb]]s. In the long-running British television series ''[[Doctor Who]]'', the [[Fourth Doctor]] and his companion [[Leela (Doctor Who)|Leela]] were cloned in a matter of seconds from DNA samples ("[[The Invisible Enemy (Doctor Who)|The Invisible Enemy]]", 1977) and then – in an apparent [[Homage (arts)|homage]] to the 1966 film ''[[Fantastic Voyage]]'' – shrunk to microscopic size to enter the Doctor's body to combat an alien virus. The clones in this story are short-lived, and can only survive a matter of minutes before they expire.<ref name="muir">{{cite book|last1=Muir|first1=John Kenneth|title=A Critical History of Doctor Who on Television|date=2007|publisher=McFarland|isbn=978-1-4766-0454-1|pages=258–9|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qMKSCgAAQBAJ&pg=PA259|access-date=4 November 2017|language=en}}</ref> Science fiction films such as ''[[The Matrix]]'' and ''Star Wars: Episode II – Attack of the Clones'' have featured scenes of human [[fetus|foetus]]es being cultured on an industrial scale in mechanical tanks.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Mumford|first1=James|title=Ethics at the Beginning of Life: A Phenomenological Critique|date=2013|publisher=OUP Oxford|isbn=978-0-19-967396-4|page=108|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UCnmRCDGJ0cC&pg=PA108|access-date=6 November 2017|language=en}}</ref>

Cloning humans from body parts is also a common theme in science fiction. Cloning features strongly among the science fiction conventions parodied in Woody Allen's ''[[Sleeper (1973 film)|Sleeper]]'', the plot of which centres around an attempt to clone an assassinated dictator from his disembodied nose.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Humber|first1=James M.|last2=Almeder|first2=Robert|title=Human Cloning|date=1998|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-1-59259-205-0|page=10|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vNGUBwAAQBAJ&pg=PA10|access-date=6 November 2017|language=en}}</ref> In the 2008 ''Doctor Who'' story "[[Journey's End (Doctor Who)|Journey's End]]", a duplicate version of the [[Tenth Doctor]] spontaneously grows from his severed hand, which had been cut off in a sword fight during an earlier episode.<ref name="smithka">{{cite book|last1=Lewis|first1=Courtland|last2=Smithka|first2=Paula|title=Doctor Who and Philosophy: Bigger on the Inside|date=2010|publisher=Open Court|isbn=978-0-8126-9725-4|pages=32–33|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ShPnLHcKqUwC&pg=PA32|access-date=4 November 2017|language=en|chapter=What's Continuity without Persistence?}}</ref>

After the death of her beloved 14-year-old [[Coton de Tulear]] named Samantha in late 2017, [[Barbra Streisand]] announced that she had cloned the dog, and was now "waiting for [the two cloned pups] to get older so [she] can see if they have [Samantha's] brown eyes and her seriousness".<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/entertainment/streisand-dog-clone-1.4555800?cmp=rss|title=Twice as nice: Barbra Streisand cloned her beloved dog and has 2 new pups|work=CBC News|access-date=1 March 2018|language=en}}</ref> The operation cost $50,000 through the pet cloning company [[ViaGen Pets|ViaGen]].<ref>{{Cite news|last=Streisand|first=Barbra|date=2 March 2018|title=Barbra Streisand Explains: Why I Cloned My Dog|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/03/02/style/barbra-streisand-cloned-her-dog.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220101/https://www.nytimes.com/2018/03/02/style/barbra-streisand-cloned-her-dog.html |archive-date=2022-01-01 |url-access=limited|access-date=23 June 2020|issn=0362-4331}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

In films such as [[Roger Spottiswoode]]'s 2000 ''[[The 6th Day]]'', which makes use of the trope of a "vast clandestine laboratory ... filled with row upon row of 'blank' human bodies kept floating in tanks of nutrient liquid or in suspended animation", clearly fear is to be incited. In Clark's view, the biotechnology is typically "given fantastic but visually arresting forms" while the science is either relegated to the background or fictionalised to suit a young audience.<ref name="Wellcome" /> Genetic engineering methods are weakly represented in film; Michael Clark, writing for [[The Wellcome Trust]], calls the portrayal of genetic engineering and biotechnology "seriously distorted"<ref name=Wellcome>{{cite web |last=Clark |first=Michael |title=Genetic themes in fiction films: Genetics meets Hollywood |url=http://genome.wellcome.ac.uk/doc_WTD023539.html |publisher=[[The Wellcome Trust]] |access-date=19 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120518055848/http://genome.wellcome.ac.uk/doc_WTD023539.html |archive-date=18 May 2012}}</ref>

In November 2025, former American football quarterback [[Tom Brady]] received a lot of criticism when he announced that his dog Junie is a clone of his late dog Lua.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/11/04/science/tom-brady-dog-cloning.html|title=Tom Brady Says He Cloned His Dog. Cue the Critics.|last1=Deb|first1=Sopan|last2=Bijaj|first2=Simar|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=4 November 2025|accessdate=7 November 2025}}</ref>

===Cloning and identity===
Science fiction has used cloning, most commonly and specifically [[human cloning]], to address questions of identity and [[eugenics]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Hopkins|first=Patrick|title=How Popular media represent cloning as an ethical problem|jstor=3527566|volume=28|issue=2|pages=6–13|doi=10.2307/3527566|pmid=9589288|journal=The Hastings Center Report|url=http://kie.georgetown.edu/nrcbl/documents/hcr/v28/h28n2p06.pdf|year=1998}}{{Dead link|date=November 2019 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.csustan.edu/honors/documents/journals/thresholds/Delacruz.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110928163727/http://www.csustan.edu/honors/documents/journals/thresholds/Delacruz.pdf |archive-date=2011-09-28 |url-status=live |title=Yvonne A. De La Cruz ''Science Fiction Storytelling and Identity: Seeing the Human Through Android Eyes'' |access-date=19 August 2012}}</ref> ''[[A Number]]'' is a 2002 play by English playwright [[Caryl Churchill]] which addresses the subject of human cloning and identity, especially [[nature and nurture]]. The story, set in the near future, is structured around the conflict between a father (Salter) and his sons (Bernard 1, Bernard 2, and Michael Black) {{Ndash}}the second two of whom are clones of the first. ''A Number'' was adapted by Caryl Churchill for television, in a co-production between the [[BBC]] and [[HBO Films]].<ref>{{cite press release| title = Uma Thurman, Rhys Ifans and Tom Wilkinson star in two plays for BBC Two| publisher = BBC| date = 19 June 2008| url = http://www.bbc.co.uk/pressoffice/pressreleases/stories/2008/06_june/19/stage.shtml| access-date = 9 September 2008 }}</ref>

In 2012, a Japanese television series named "Bunshin" was created. The story's main character, Mariko, is a woman studying child welfare in Hokkaido. She grew up always doubtful about the love from her mother, who looked nothing like her and who died nine years before. One day, she finds some of her mother's belongings at a relative's house, and heads to Tokyo to seek out the truth behind her birth. She later discovered that she was a clone.<ref>{{cite web | title=Review of Bunshin |url =https://doramaworld.blogspot.com/2012/06/review-of-bunshin.html|date =9 June 2012}}</ref>

In the 2013 television series ''[[Orphan Black]]'', cloning is used as a scientific study on the behavioral adaptation of the clones.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt2234222/|title=Orphan Black (TV Series 2013– )|website=IMDb|access-date=3 May 2015}}</ref> In a similar vein, the book ''[[The Double (Saramago novel)|The Double]]'' by Nobel Prize winner [[José Saramago]] explores the emotional experience of a man who discovers that he is a clone.<ref>{{cite news |first=John |last=Banville |title='The Double': The Tears of a Clone|work=The New York Times |date=10 October 2004|access-date=14 January 2015 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2004/10/10/books/review/10BANV01.html }}</ref>

===Cloning as resurrection===
Cloning has been used in fiction as a way of recreating historical figures. In the 1976 [[Ira Levin]] novel ''[[The Boys from Brazil (novel)|The Boys from Brazil]]'' and its [[The Boys from Brazil (film)|1978 film adaptation]], [[Josef Mengele]] uses cloning to create copies of [[Adolf Hitler]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0077269/|title=The Boys from Brazil (1978)|author=Christian Lee Pyle |date=12 October 1978|website=IMDb|access-date=3 May 2015}}</ref>

The [[Norman Spinrad]]'s satirical [[The Iron Dream]], published in 1972, concludes with 300 seven-foot-tall, blond, super-intelligent all-male SS clones in suspended animation launched into space to begin the Hitler analog's [[galactic empire]] in the aftermath of a genocidal [[race war]]. (They had won a [[Pyrrhic victory]], the subhumans' leader having as his last act detonated a [[doomsday weapon]], specifically a [[cobalt bomb]], irredeemably contaminated the [[gene pool]]).<ref name="leguin">{{Cite web |url=https://www.depauw.edu/sfs/backissues/1/leguin1art.htm |title=On Norman Spinrad's ''The Iron Dream'' |last=Le Guin |first=Ursula K. |author-link=Ursula K. Le Guin |date=Spring 1973 |website=Science Fiction Studies |access-date=2007-02-09}}</ref>

In [[Michael Crichton]]'s 1990 novel ''[[Jurassic Park (novel)|Jurassic Park]]'', which spawned a [[Jurassic Park (franchise)|series of ''Jurassic Park'' feature films]], the bioengineering company InGen develops a technique to resurrect extinct species of dinosaurs by creating cloned creatures using DNA extracted from [[fossil]]s. The cloned dinosaurs are used to populate the Jurassic Park [[Animal theme park|wildlife park]] for the entertainment of visitors. The scheme goes disastrously wrong when the dinosaurs escape their enclosures.<ref name="cohen">{{cite book|last1=Cohen|first1=Daniel|title=Cloning|date=2002|publisher=Millbrook Press|isbn=978-0-7613-2802-5|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TpBEOaHhb4oC&pg=PA73|access-date=4 November 2017|language=en}}</ref>

===Cloning for warfare===
The use of cloning for military purposes has also been explored in several fictional works. In ''Doctor Who'', an alien race of armour-clad, warlike beings called [[Sontaran]]s was introduced in the 1973 serial "[[The Time Warrior]]". Sontarans are depicted as squat, bald creatures who have been genetically engineered for combat. Their weak spot is a "probic vent", a small socket at the back of their neck which is associated with the cloning process.<ref name="thompson">{{cite book|last1=Thompson|first1=Dave|title=Doctor Who FAQ: All That's Left to Know About the Most Famous Time Lord in the Universe|date=2013|publisher=Hal Leonard Corporation|isbn=978-1-4803-4295-8|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QcEXAAAAQBAJ&pg=PT119|access-date=4 November 2017|language=en}}</ref> The concept of cloned soldiers being bred for combat was revisited in "[[The Doctor's Daughter]]" (2008), when the Doctor's DNA is used to create a female warrior called [[Jenny (Doctor Who)|Jenny]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Barr|first1=Jason|last2=Mustachio|first2=Camille D. G.|title=The Language of Doctor Who: From Shakespeare to Alien Tongues|date=2014|publisher=Rowman & Littlefield|isbn=978-1-4422-3481-9|page=219|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ImuYAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA219|access-date=5 November 2017|language=en}}</ref>

The 1977 film ''[[Star Wars (film)|Star Wars]]'' was set against the backdrop of a historical conflict called the [[Clone Wars]]. The events of this war were not fully explored until the prequel films ''[[Star Wars: Episode II – Attack of the Clones|Attack of the Clones]]'' (2002) and ''[[Star Wars: Episode III – Revenge of the Sith|Revenge of the Sith]]'' (2005), which depict a [[Space warfare in fiction|space war]] waged by a massive army of heavily armoured [[clone trooper]]s that leads to the foundation of the [[Galactic Empire (Star Wars)|Galactic Empire]]. Cloned soldiers are "manufactured" on an industrial scale, genetically conditioned for obedience and combat effectiveness. It is also revealed that the popular character [[Boba Fett]] originated as a clone of [[Jango Fett]], a mercenary who served as the genetic template for the clone troopers.<ref name="mcdonald">{{cite book|last1=McDonald|first1=Paul F.|title=The Star Wars Heresies: Interpreting the Themes, Symbols and Philosophies of Episodes I, II and III|date=2013|publisher=McFarland|isbn=978-0-7864-7181-2|pages=167–171|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Wf4CAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA167|access-date=4 November 2017|language=en|chapter=The Clones}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1185834/|title=Star Wars: The Clone Wars (2008)|date=15 August 2008|website=IMDb|access-date=3 May 2015}}</ref>

===Cloning for exploitation===
A recurring sub-theme of cloning fiction is the use of clones as a supply of [[Organ (anatomy)|organs]] for [[Organ transplant|transplantation]]. The 2005 [[Kazuo Ishiguro]] novel ''[[Never Let Me Go (novel)|Never Let Me Go]]'' and the [[Never Let Me Go (2010 film)|2010 film adaption]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1334260/|title=Never Let Me Go (2010)|date=11 February 2011|website=IMDb|access-date=3 May 2015}}</ref> are set in an [[alternate history]] in which cloned humans are created for the sole purpose of providing organ donations to naturally born humans, despite the fact that they are fully sentient and self-aware. The 2005 film ''[[The Island (2005 film)|The Island]]''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0399201/|title=The Island (2005)|date=22 July 2005|website=IMDb|access-date=3 May 2015}}</ref> revolves around a similar plot, with the exception that the clones are unaware of the reason for their existence.

The exploitation of human clones for dangerous and undesirable work was examined in the 2009 British science fiction film ''[[Moon (2009 film)|Moon]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1182345/|title=Moon (2009)|date=17 July 2009|website=IMDb|access-date=3 May 2015}}</ref> In the futuristic novel ''[[Cloud Atlas (novel)|Cloud Atlas]]'' and subsequent [[Cloud Atlas (film)|film]], one of the story lines focuses on a genetically engineered fabricant clone named Sonmi~451, one of millions raised in an artificial "wombtank", destined to serve from birth. She is one of thousands created for manual and [[emotional labor]]; Sonmi herself works as a server in a restaurant. She later discovers that the sole source of food for clones, called 'Soap', is manufactured from the clones themselves.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.technewsdaily.com/8402-human-clones-cloud-atlas.html|title=Technology News – 2017 Innovations and Future Tech|access-date=15 December 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140105103230/http://www.technewsdaily.com/8402-human-clones-cloud-atlas.html|archive-date=5 January 2014}}</ref>

In the film ''[[Us (2019 film)|Us]]'', at some point prior to the 1980s, the US Government creates clones of every citizen of the United States with the intention of using them to control their original counterparts, akin to [[voodoo doll]]s. This fails, as they were able to copy bodies, but unable to copy the souls of those they cloned. The project is abandoned and the clones are trapped exactly mirroring their above-ground counterparts' actions for generations. In the present day, the clones launch a surprise attack and manage to complete a mass-genocide of their unaware counterparts.<ref>{{cite web| url= https://www.denofgeek.com/us/movies/us/280039/us-the-tethered-explained| title= Us: Who Are the Tethered? |author= Daniel Kurland | date = 23 May 2019 | access-date= 11 July 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url = https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/heat-vision/us-ending-explained-could-be-a-sequel-1196643| title= 'Us' Ending Explained: Could There Be A Sequel? | author = Jason Spiegel | website= [[The Hollywood Reporter]] | date = 23 March 2019 | access-date = 11 July 2019}}</ref>
